clue.text: Pleasant comedy only half viewed because of the programme

indicators.note: only half of the word comedy is seen, so its first three letters are kept

parts.note: taken as written, before half of it is dropped
for can mean on account of, as in 'jumped for joy'
a table is a schedule or timetable, as a programme can be

explanation.surface: A viewer finds the comedy agreeable even though they only caught half of it because of the programme scheduling.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfortable describes something easy and agreeable, a close synonym of pleasant.

clue.text: Soft-soap powder to advocate using

parts.note: curry powder is the spice mix, so powder stands for curry
to favour a plan is to support or advocate it
with can mean by means of, as in 'cut with a knife'

explanation.surface: A sales pitch for soap powder, recommending you use it.
explanation.walkthrough: Soft-soap and powder both suggest laundry products, but soft-soap is the verb for flattering someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To soft-soap someone is to flatter them to win advantage, which is the idiom meaning ingratiate oneself.

clue.text: Opera singer gets blame, unhappily

indicators.note: something going unhappily goes wrong, so the letters of blame are put in a different order

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A diva is held responsible for something that went badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Nellie Melba was a famous Australian soprano, remembered also in peach Melba and Melba toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Nellie Melba was a celebrated operatic soprano, so she is an example of an opera singer.

clue.text: Bare bones of dead family

parts.note: out can mean extinguished or finished, like a fire that is out
a line is a family lineage, as in 'the royal line'

explanation.surface: Only skeletons remain of a family that has died.
explanation.definitionFit: An outline gives just the main points of something, which is the idiom 'bare bones' as a summary.

clue.text: This point of view ought to attract half of them

indicators.note: ought draws the other piece to itself, so that piece sits right in front of it
only the first two of the four letters of them are taken

parts.note: taken as written, before it is cut in half
taken as written

explanation.surface: A claim that this opinion should win over half of a group of people.
explanation.definitionFit: A thought can be an opinion or idea someone holds, which is a synonym of point of view.

clue.text: Mini lecture put into immature speech

parts.note: baby as an adjective means very small, like mini
a talk is an informal lecture

explanation.surface: A short lecture is delivered in childish language.
explanation.definitionFit: Baby talk is the simplified speech used by or to infants, so it is literally the speech of the immature.

clue.text: Long drawn out hate on our estate

indicators.note: the letters are pulled out of their order and laid down anew

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A long, tedious feud over who hates the family property.
explanation.walkthrough: Long looks like an adjective, but here it is the verb meaning yearn; 'drawn out' looks like part of the same picture of length.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat one's heart out is the idiom for pining or yearning bitterly for something, the verb sense of long.

clue.text: Is impatient to behead hags

indicators.note: cutting off the head removes the first letter of the word for hags

parts.note: witches are often called hags in fairy tales

explanation.surface: Someone cannot wait to cut the heads off some old crones.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who itches to do something is eager and restless, an idiom for being impatient.

clue.text: Contestant is one who spends about a pound

indicators.note: the word for a spender goes around the pound sign, enclosing it

parts.note: a payer is someone who hands over money
L, from Latin libra, is the pound sign

explanation.surface: A game show entrant turns out to be someone who spends roughly a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: A player is anyone taking part in a game or match, a synonym of contestant.

clue.text: Alter mixture going into dry little cake

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed inside the abbreviation for dry

parts.note: TT means teetotal, someone who abstains from alcohol, as in a dry state

indicators.note: the letters of alter are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A baker changes the mix before it goes into a dry cupcake.
explanation.walkthrough: TT stands for teetotal; 'dry' looks like it describes the cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A tartlet is a small tart, a little pastry treat which the clue loosely calls a cake.

clue.text: Bypass is the part spoken about

indicators.note: the word for spoken goes around the word for part

parts.note: oral means spoken rather than written
a bit is a part or piece

explanation.surface: A query about which section of a road is under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: An orbital is a British ring road around a city, like the M25 around London.
explanation.definitionFit: A bypass and an orbital are both roads routed around a town to keep traffic out of the centre.

clue.text: Performing like wild boxers or farm workers?

definitions.meaning: a haymaker is a wild swinging punch, so a boxer throwing them is doing this
farm hands cutting and drying grass in summer are doing this too

explanation.walkthrough: Haymaker is boxing slang for a big looping punch, so one word covers both the brawler and the farm hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the swinging of wild punches and the harvesting of grass for fodder share this single name.

clue.text: Cheap time in New York

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A budget trip to New York.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinny describes something flimsy and badly made, like thin metal, so it suggests shoddy and low-quality.

clue.text: Playwright's maxim about hospital

indicators.note: the word for a saying goes around the hospital letter

parts.note: a saw is an old saying or proverb

explanation.surface: A dramatist's motto concerns a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard Shaw was the Irish dramatist who wrote Pygmalion, so he is an example of a playwright.

clue.text: Perhaps manure once fires relit

indicators.note: signals the letters of fires relit as they were before, in a former order that must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Muck heaps that had smouldered get set alight again.
explanation.walkthrough: Relit looks like the anagram signal but belongs to the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Manure is one example of a fertiliser, a substance spread on soil to feed plants, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Cake decoration, lovely one

parts.note: angelic means beautiful or sweet, like an angel

explanation.surface: A cake topping that is charming and unique.
explanation.definitionFit: Angelica is a herb whose candied green stems are a traditional decoration on cakes.

clue.text: British have money for these sandwiches

definitions.note: a plural description standing for a type of bread used to make them

parts.note: to own something is to have it
bread is slang for money

explanation.surface: Britons pay for their sandwiches.
explanation.definitionFit: Brown bread is wholemeal loaf, the type used to make these sandwiches.

clue.text: Distressed bather calling for air

indicators.note: something distressed is disturbed, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A swimmer in trouble shouts for air.
explanation.definitionFit: A breath is a lungful of air, so the two are close in sense.

clue.text: Reginald needs a friend — like a Royal

parts.note: Reg is the usual short form of the name Reginald
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Reginald wants a companion who is like a royal.
explanation.definitionFit: Regally means in the manner of a king or queen, a royal person.

clue.text: Fat Ida turns up to model

indicators.note: in a down clue the name is read from the bottom upwards, so it is reversed

parts.note: taken as written, then read backwards
to pose is to model for an artist

explanation.surface: A woman named Ida, overweight, arrives to sit for a portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: Adipose is the technical term for fatty tissue, so it means fat.

clue.text: Career shows sign of distress

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to rush wildly along
second meaning: a drop from the eye when crying

explanation.walkthrough: Career looks like a noun for a job, but it is the verb meaning hurtle; the word rhymes with 'bear' in that sense and with 'beer' in the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To tear is to dash along fast, as a career is; a tear is shed when upset.

clue.text: A bit of salad for artist with attractive girl

parts.note: dish is dated slang for a good-looking person

explanation.surface: An artist shares a light lunch with a pretty woman.
explanation.walkthrough: RA is a Royal Academician, a member of Britain's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: A radish is a crunchy red root vegetable often eaten raw as one ingredient of a salad.

clue.text: No head on beer? That is strange

indicators.note: the drink loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written, before its first letter goes
i.e. is the abbreviation of Latin id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: A drinker complains that a pint without froth is odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' looks like the froth on beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eerie means weird and unsettling, a synonym of strange.

clue.text: Flashed Guardian leader — rubbish by editor

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the word Guardian supplies its first letter
litter is rubbish dropped in public

explanation.surface: The Guardian's editorial is denounced as trash by its editor.
explanation.walkthrough: A newspaper leader is an editorial, which is what the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Glittered means sparkled with bright points of light, so it is a synonym of flashed.

clue.text: Pitiable creature found lying in bath in Guildford

indicators.note: the letters are lying inside the words that follow, spanning their break

parts.note: the answer runs across the end of bath, all of in and the start of Guildford

explanation.surface: A poor animal is discovered in a bathtub in a Surrey town.
explanation.walkthrough: Guildford is a county town in Surrey, south-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Thing is used of a person or animal to express pity, as in 'poor thing'.

clue.text: Insignificant six involved in lawsuit

indicators.note: the Roman numeral goes inside the word for a court hearing

parts.note: a trial is the hearing of a lawsuit in court

explanation.surface: Six people caught up in a court case play only minor roles.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial means of little importance, a direct synonym of insignificant.

clue.text: Menacing black coat with front not seen by us

indicators.note: the first letter of the cloak's name is hidden from view and dropped

parts.note: a domino is a loose hooded cloak, traditionally black, worn at masquerades
taken as written

explanation.surface: A figure in a black coat lurks, its face hidden from us.
explanation.definitionFit: Ominous means threatening that something bad will happen, a synonym of menacing.

clue.text: Pugilist, difficult to clout

parts.note: heavy can mean hard going, as in heavy reading
weight means influence, as clout does

explanation.surface: A boxer who is hard to land a punch on.
explanation.walkthrough: Clout looks like a blow, which fits the boxer, but it is the influence sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavyweight is a boxer in the heaviest weight division, so it is a kind of pugilist.
